abstract: Intranasal drug delivery is being explored as an alternative approach to overcome the blood-brain barrier in the treatment of central nervous system diseases. However, little is known about how therapeutics administered through this route affect human olfactory tissue. Here, we develop human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived olfactory sensory organoids that reproduce key cellular and functional features of the developing olfactory system. Over three months of differentiation, the organoids acquire diverse neuronal and glial-associated populations, including cells expressing markers of olfactory sensory neurons and interneurons. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing shows changes in cellular composition and lineage-associated transcriptional programs during maturation, while comparison with a human fetal nasal atlas identifies shared neural populations and developmental signatures. Alongside these molecular changes, the organoids develop spontaneous electrical activity and coordinated network bursting. Exposure to the glioma-relevant kinase inhibitors Dasatinib, Trametinib, and Selumetinib produces distinct changes in neuronal network activity, demonstrating the ability of the model to capture compound-associated functional responses. Together, these findings establish a human Olfactory Sensory Organoid system for investigating olfactory development and evaluating how therapeutics may affect olfactory neural tissue during intranasal drug administration.
